items.stimulus:
For much of the twentieth century, courts treated a confident eyewitness as one of the most persuasive forms of evidence available. Research in cognitive psychology, however, has steadily undermined the assumption that memory works like a recording that can simply be replayed. Each act of remembering involves reconstruction: the brain keeps fragments of an experience and fills the gaps with expectations, inferences and information acquired later.

Laboratory studies show how easily this process can be steered. In a typical experiment, volunteers watch a short clip of a theft in a shop and then read a summary of the event that wrongly mentions a detail, such as the thief wearing a cap. When later asked to describe what they saw, a substantial share include the cap in their own account, and few can say where the detail came from. Information supplied after an event can therefore become blended with the original memory.

Conditions at the time of the event matter as well. Poor lighting, brief exposure and long viewing distances all reduce accuracy. When a weapon is visible, witnesses tend to fix their attention on it and recall less about the person holding it. Identifications of strangers from a different ethnic group are, on average, less accurate than identifications of people from one's own group.

Confidence is a more complicated matter. The certainty a witness expresses in the courtroom, often months after the event, is a poor guide to accuracy, because it can grow with repeated retelling and with encouraging feedback, such as being told that one picked the suspect. By contrast, confidence recorded at a first, fairly conducted identification carries considerably more information. For this reason, many researchers recommend that line-ups be run by an officer who does not know which person is the suspect, that witnesses be warned the culprit may not be present, and that their confidence be written down in their own words before anything else is said to them.

Reviews of convictions later overturned on the basis of DNA evidence have found mistaken eyewitness identification to be a contributing factor in a large proportion of those cases.

items.stimulus:
When European explorers reached the scattered islands of the Pacific, they found people living on small areas of land separated by hundreds or thousands of kilometres of open ocean. Some later scholars, unable to imagine deliberate voyages without compass or chart, concluded that the islands must have been settled by canoes blown off course. That view now seems far less convincing, partly because computer simulations of drifting vessels showed that many islands were very unlikely to have been reached by chance alone, and partly because the navigational knowledge itself was recorded and revived.

Wayfinders read the night sky as a moving guide. A given star rises at the same point on the horizon each night, so a navigator who had memorised the rising and setting points of many stars could hold a course by steering towards one that was low in the right direction, replacing it with another as it climbed too high to be useful. During the day and under cloud, the ocean itself became the guide. Long, regular swells generated by distant weather systems keep their direction for days, and an experienced navigator could feel their rhythm through the hull, noticing when a new swell crossed the dominant one or when an island bent and reflected them.

Land could also be detected well before it was visible. Certain seabirds fish at sea by day and return to land at dusk, so their flight paths in the evening point towards an island. Clouds tend to pile up and linger over high islands, and the underside of a cloud above a shallow lagoon may take on a faint green tinge. Because such signs extend the area over which an island can be detected to many times its actual width, a navigator did not need to strike a tiny target exactly: it was enough to reach the wider zone of clues surrounding it.

In 1976 a double-hulled voyaging canoe sailed more than 4,000 kilometres from Hawaii to Tahiti, guided by a Micronesian navigator who used no instruments. The voyage did not prove how every ancient journey was made, but it showed that such journeys were entirely possible.

items.stimulus:
Many eucalypts survive fires that would kill most other trees. Beneath their bark lie dormant buds connected to the living tissue of the trunk and branches. The thick bark of many species insulates these buds from the heat, and within weeks of a fire they can burst into growth, clothing blackened trunks in dense shoots of new leaves. This epicormic resprouting allows a tree to rebuild its canopy without starting again from the ground.

Some species carry a second form of insurance below the soil. A swollen woody structure at the base of the stem, known as a lignotuber, stores buds and reserves of starch. If the stems above are destroyed, shoots can emerge from the lignotuber, and many low, multi-stemmed eucalypts of drier country regenerate in this way after repeated fires.

Not every eucalypt resprouts. Mountain ash, among the tallest flowering plants on Earth, has relatively thin bark and is usually killed outright by an intense fire. Its forests instead regenerate from seed. The trees hold their seed in woody capsules in the canopy, and the heat of a fire triggers a mass release onto the ground below. The ash bed left behind is rich in nutrients and clear of competing plants, and the sheer number of seeds falling at once means that seed-eating insects can consume only a fraction of them. The result is a dense stand of seedlings, all of the same age.

This strategy has a weakness. Young mountain ash trees need roughly two decades before they produce seed of their own. If a second severe fire sweeps through a regenerating stand before then, there may be no seed left to replace the trees, and the forest can give way to shrubland or wattle. Ecologists are concerned that in some regions fires are now returning more often, shortening the interval between them.
items.question: Mountain ash seedlings grow more quickly than the new shoots of resprouting eucalypts.

items.stimulus:
Planning food for an early twentieth-century Antarctic sledging journey was an exercise in compromise. Every kilogram had to be hauled across the ice by dogs, ponies or the explorers themselves, so rations were chosen for the energy they packed into the smallest weight. The staple was pemmican, a dense mixture of dried meat and fat, eaten with hard biscuits, sugar, butter and cocoa or tea. Fat was prized because, weight for weight, it supplies more than twice the energy of protein or carbohydrate.

Even so, the rations usually fell short. Modern estimates suggest that men hauling heavy sledges in extreme cold may have used 6,000 kilocalories or more each day, while many daily rations supplied around 4,500. Over weeks, the gap showed itself in constant hunger, weight loss and growing weakness, which in turn made men slower and more prone to injury.

The other danger was scurvy. Expedition doctors knew that fresh food protected against it, though the vitamin responsible had not yet been identified, and many parties ate fresh seal and penguin meat while at base. On long journeys, however, such food was rarely available, and preserved rations offered little protection.

Some leaders built more flexibility into their plans. Expeditions that relied on dogs could, in a calculated way, feed weaker animals to the others and to the men as the loads lightened, turning transport into food. Whatever the method, the margins were narrow, and a few days lost to blizzards could turn an adequate ration into a dangerous one.

items.stimulus:
The human large intestine is home to trillions of microorganisms, most of them bacteria, collectively known as the gut microbiome. Far from being passive passengers, these microbes carry out chemical work that the human body cannot do on its own. Much dietary fibre, for example, passes through the stomach and small intestine undigested because humans lack the enzymes to break it down. In the large intestine, bacteria ferment this fibre and release short-chain fatty acids, one of which, butyrate, is a major energy source for the cells lining the colon.

Diet shapes which microbes flourish. In controlled studies, volunteers who switched between a plant-heavy diet and one based largely on meat and cheese showed measurable changes in their gut bacteria within a few days. People who eat a wide variety of plant foods tend to host a more diverse community of microbes, and lower diversity has been associated with a number of chronic conditions.

Interpreting these associations is harder than reporting them. Someone with a diverse microbiome may also exercise more, sleep better or take fewer medicines, any of which could influence health independently. Many of the clearest demonstrations that microbes can cause changes in their host come from experiments on mice raised without any gut bacteria, and results in mice do not always carry over to people. Commercial products promising to reshape the microbiome often run ahead of this evidence.

For now, the advice that follows most securely from the research is unglamorous: eating more fibre from a range of plant sources feeds the microbes that appear to be most useful, whatever else remains uncertain.

items.stimulus:
Every second, tens of billions of neutrinos produced by nuclear reactions in the Sun pass through each square centimetre of your body, and almost none of them leave any trace. Neutrinos are among the most abundant particles in the universe, yet they are notoriously difficult to catch.

The reason lies in how weakly they interact with ordinary matter. Neutrinos carry no electric charge, so they are unaffected by the electromagnetic forces that hold atoms together and that most detectors rely on to register a passing particle. Their mass is so tiny that for decades many physicists assumed it was zero. Apart from gravity, they respond only to the weak nuclear force, which acts over extremely short distances. A neutrino can therefore travel through the whole Earth with only a small chance of striking anything at all.

Detecting them is consequently a numbers game. Because any single neutrino is very unlikely to interact, experiments use enormous quantities of target material, so that among the vast number passing through, a handful will collide with a nucleus or an electron each day. One detector in Japan holds 50,000 tonnes of ultra-pure water, and another experiment monitors a cubic kilometre of ice beneath the South Pole. When a neutrino does interact, it can produce a fast-moving charged particle that gives off a faint cone of blue light, which sensitive light sensors record.

These detectors are usually built deep underground or under ice. The rock or ice above them absorbs most of the particles produced when cosmic rays strike the atmosphere, which would otherwise swamp the rare neutrino signals. Neutrinos themselves pass through the overlying layers without difficulty.

items.stimulus:
Over the past decade, employers in several countries have experimented with a four-day working week. The most common model keeps pay at its usual level while cutting hours by about a fifth, on the understanding that staff will maintain their usual output. Supporters describe this as a bargain in which time once lost to unproductive meetings and distractions is reclaimed as a day off.

Reported results have been striking. In one widely publicised trial involving around sixty organisations, the large majority chose to continue the arrangement after the trial ended, and employees reported less stress, better sleep and fewer days off sick. Managers in several trials said that revenue held steady, and some reported that staff were less likely to resign.

Yet the design of these trials limits what they can show. Organisations volunteered to take part, and a firm confident enough to try a shorter week may already have had flexible management, motivated staff or work that is easy to reorganise. Few trials compared participating firms with similar firms that kept a five-day week, so it is hard to separate the effect of the shorter week from changes happening across the economy at the same time. Much of the evidence on wellbeing comes from surveys of employees who knew they were in a trial and who stood to keep a benefit they valued, which may colour their answers.

The arrangement also suits some kinds of work better than others. Where output depends on staff being present for set hours, as in hospitals, schools or shops, a shorter week for each employee usually means hiring more people or extending rosters, and the savings from reorganised meetings are small.

None of this means the trials have failed. It means their results describe what happened in particular, self-selected workplaces, and the question of whether a four-day week would work across a whole economy remains open.

items.stimulus:
Imagine a witness in a trial who says that her neighbour told her she had seen the defendant leave a building at midnight. The witness saw nothing herself; she is repeating what someone else said. Courts in common-law countries, including Australia, have long treated evidence of this kind, known as hearsay, with suspicion, and the general rule is that it cannot be used to prove that what was said is true.

The reasons are practical. A person giving evidence in court normally does so under oath, and the opposing side can test the account through cross-examination, probing whether the witness could see clearly, remembers accurately or has a motive to lie. The court can also observe how the witness answers. When a statement is relayed second-hand, none of these safeguards applies to the person who originally made it. The neighbour may have been mistaken, may have been joking or may have been misheard, and there is no way to question her.

The rule is narrower than it first appears. It applies only when the earlier statement is offered as proof of the facts it asserts. If the same words are offered for a different purpose, for example to show that a warning was given and that someone therefore knew of a danger, the evidence may be admitted, because the issue is whether the words were spoken, not whether they were accurate.

The rule also has many exceptions, which differ between jurisdictions. Common examples include records made in the ordinary course of business and certain statements made by a person who was dying. Critics argue that the resulting body of law is so complicated that it confuses juries and lawyers alike, and some jurisdictions have relaxed the rule in civil cases while keeping it stricter in criminal trials.

items.stimulus:
Imagine a witness in a trial who says that her neighbour told her she had seen the defendant leave a building at midnight. The witness saw nothing herself; she is repeating what someone else said. Courts in common-law countries, including Australia, have long treated evidence of this kind, known as hearsay, with suspicion, and the general rule is that it cannot be used to prove that what was said is true.

The reasons are practical. A person giving evidence in court normally does so under oath, and the opposing side can test the account through cross-examination, probing whether the witness could see clearly, remembers accurately or has a motive to lie. The court can also observe how the witness answers. When a statement is relayed second-hand, none of these safeguards applies to the person who originally made it. The neighbour may have been mistaken, may have been joking or may have been misheard, and there is no way to question her.

The rule is narrower than it first appears. It applies only when the earlier statement is offered as proof of the facts it asserts. If the same words are offered for a different purpose, for example to show that a warning was given and that someone therefore knew of a danger, the evidence may be admitted, because the issue is whether the words were spoken, not whether they were accurate.

The rule also has many exceptions, which differ between jurisdictions. Common examples include records made in the ordinary course of business and certain statements made by a person who was dying. Critics argue that the resulting body of law is so complicated that it confuses juries and lawyers alike, and some jurisdictions have relaxed the rule in civil cases while keeping it stricter in criminal trials.

In 1971 the American philosopher John Rawls set out a thought experiment intended to help people reason about what a fair society would look like. Suppose you were asked to choose the basic rules of a society without knowing what position you would occupy in it. You would not know whether you would be wealthy or poor, healthy or chronically ill, gifted or ordinary, nor which beliefs you would hold or which group you would belong to. Rawls called this condition of deliberately limited knowledge the veil of ignorance.

The point of the device is to remove the temptation to design rules that favour oneself. A person who knows she will inherit a large farm might argue for low taxes on land; a person who knows he will rent all his life might argue the opposite. Behind the veil, neither can tailor the rules to a known situation, so whatever rules are chosen must be ones that a person could accept from any position.

Rawls argued that people choosing in these conditions would reach two main conclusions. First, they would insist on equal basic liberties for everyone, such as freedom of conscience and of speech, and would not trade these away for economic gains. Second, they would accept differences in income and wealth only where those differences work to the benefit of the worst-off members of society, for example by rewarding work that raises everyone's living standards. His reasoning was that, with so much at stake and no reliable way to estimate one's chances, a sensible chooser would want to make the worst possible outcome as tolerable as it could be.

items.stimulus:
Facial-recognition systems are used in two quite different ways. In verification, a system checks whether a face matches one stored image, as when a phone unlocks for its owner or an airport gate compares a traveller with the photograph in her passport. In identification, it compares a face against a database that may contain millions of images, looking for possible matches. The second task is far more demanding, because every additional comparison is another opportunity for a false match.

Every system must also balance two kinds of error. If it is set to accept matches readily, it will rarely fail to recognise the right person but will more often match the wrong one; if it is set strictly, the reverse happens. Where the threshold is placed depends on the purpose. A phone owner who is not recognised can simply type a passcode, whereas a false match in a police search may lead to an innocent person being questioned.

Accuracy has improved dramatically over the past decade, and the best systems now outperform most people at matching photographs of unfamiliar faces taken in good conditions. Yet independent testing has repeatedly found that error rates are not the same for everyone. A large evaluation of commercial algorithms by a United States government standards agency reported that many produced more false matches for some demographic groups than for others, with differences linked to age, sex and ethnicity. Importantly, the size of these gaps varied widely between algorithms, and the most accurate systems showed much smaller differences. A common explanation is that some systems were trained on collections of images in which certain groups were under-represented, though image quality and camera settings also play a part.

These findings suggest that facial recognition should not be judged as a single technology. Whether a particular system is acceptable depends on which algorithm is used, how it was tested, where its threshold is set, and whether a person checks its suggestions before anyone acts on them. Blanket praise and blanket condemnation both miss these distinctions.

items.stimulus:
For most of the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries, Italian panel paintings were made with egg tempera. Pigments ground to a fine powder were mixed with egg yolk and water, and the paint was applied to wooden panels coated with a smooth white ground of gesso. Tempera dries within minutes, which made it practical in a busy workshop, but it also shaped the way artists worked. Because colours could not be blended once they were on the panel, painters built up forms with many small, overlapping strokes, gradually shading from light to dark. The finished surface is matt and luminous, and it has proved remarkably durable.

Oil paint, in which pigments are bound with a drying oil such as linseed or walnut, behaves very differently. It may take days to dry, so adjacent colours can be softened into one another and changes made long after the first layer was laid down. Thin, transparent layers called glazes can be built up over one another, giving deep shadows and rich colour. Oil had been known for centuries, but painters in the Low Countries refined its use in the early fifteenth century, and their results impressed Italian patrons and artists.

The change in Italy was gradual rather than sudden. Many painters of the later fifteenth century combined the two media, laying in a design with tempera and finishing it with oil glazes. C는 '반납할 이유가 전혀 없다'는 과장으로, 다음 대출 제한이나 분실 시 배상 같은 다른 이유를 무시한다. → 정답 D

items.stimulus: All of the photographers at the Wexmoor Country Show are registered with the show office. Some photographers at the show are judges' assistants. All judges' assistants wear red armbands. Nobody registered with the show office entered the photography competition.
items.question: Place Yes if the conclusion follows. Place No if the conclusion does not follow.

statements.text: Some people wearing red armbands entered the photography competition.
Some people wearing red armbands are registered with the show office.
All judges' assistants are registered with the show office.
Some judges' assistants did not enter the photography competition.
No judges' assistant entered the photography competition.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 사진가 ⊂ 등록자, 사진가이면서 심사 보조인 사람이 존재, 심사 보조 ⊂ 빨간 완장, 등록자와 대회 참가자는 겹치지 않는다. 2) 2번: 사진가이면서 심사 보조인 사람은 빨간 완장을 차고 등록되어 있으므로 성립한다. 4번: 그 사람은 등록자이므로 대회에 참가하지 않았고, 따라서 대회에 참가하지 않은 심사 보조가 있다. 3) 1번: 사진가가 아닌 심사 보조가 대회에 참가했을 수도, 안 했을 수도 있어 판단할 수 없다. 3번: 사진가가 아닌 심사 보조는 등록 여부를 알 수 없다. 5번: 사진가가 아닌 심사 보조가 참가했을 가능성을 배제할 수 없다. → 정답 1 No, 2 Yes, 3 No, 4 Yes, 5 No

items.stimulus: A two-circle Venn diagram shows the 25 bakers who belong to the Ellerby Farmers' Cooperative. One circle is 'sells bread' and the other is 'sells cakes'. The diagram shows 9 bakers in the bread circle only, 5 in the overlap, 7 in the cakes circle only and 4 outside both circles.
items.question: Which of the following statements is supported by the diagram?

options.text: More bakers sell bread than sell cakes.
Most of the bakers sell both bread and cakes.
Every baker who sells cakes also sells bread.
Exactly half of the bakers sell cakes.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 빵을 파는 사람은 9 + 5 = 14명, 케이크를 파는 사람은 5 + 7 = 12명이다. 14 > 12이므로 A가 맞다. 2) 오답: B는 둘 다 파는 사람이 25명 중 5명뿐이라 과반이 아니다. C는 케이크만 파는 7명이 있으므로 틀렸다. D는 12/25 = 48%로 정확히 절반이 아니다(25명은 홀수라 정확히 절반이 될 수도 없다). 3) 겹치는 영역(5명)을 두 원에 모두 넣어 세는 것이 핵심이다. → 정답 A

items.stimulus: Six cyclists, Anouk, Bastien, Calloway, Dagny, Emrys and Fenella, each leave their gear in a different locker at the Marrowfield craft fair. The lockers are numbered 1 to 6 in a single row, and each cyclist uses exactly one. Dagny's locker number is double Bastien's. Emrys's locker is next to Fenella's. Calloway's locker number is odd and higher than Anouk's. Bastien is not in locker 1. Fenella's locker number is higher than Dagny's.
items.question: Which of the following must be true?

options.text: Anouk's locker is next to Dagny's.
Calloway's locker is next to Dagny's.

items.explanation_ko: 1) Dagny = 2 × Bastien이고 Bastien은 1번이 아니므로 (B, D)는 (2, 4) 또는 (3, 6)이다. (3, 6)이면 Fenella가 Dagny보다 높을 수 없으므로 Bastien 2, Dagny 4다. 2) Fenella는 4보다 높고 Emrys와 붙어 있으므로 둘이 5·6을 차지한다(순서는 정해지지 않음). 남은 1·3에서 Calloway는 홀수이면서 Anouk보다 높으므로 Calloway 3, Anouk 1이다. 3) 가능한 배치는 Emrys·Fenella 순서만 다른 두 가지다. Calloway(3)와 Dagny(4)는 항상 이웃이다. 오답: A와 B는 가능하지만 반드시 참은 아니고, C는 Anouk 1과 Dagny 4가 떨어져 있어 항상 거짓이다. → 정답 D

items.stimulus: Should new sports stadiums be built with public money?
items.question: Select the strongest argument from the statements below.

options.text: Yes, because a successful home team gives residents a sense of local pride and something enjoyable to watch at weekends.
No, because studies have generally found that new stadiums add little to local economies, as spending mostly shifts from other local leisure.
Yes, because building a large stadium creates many jobs for local construction workers and suppliers while the work is being carried out over several years.
No, because some fans behave badly on match days and cause noise and litter in the streets near the stadium.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 쟁점은 공공 자금 투입이 그만한 공적 이익을 내는가이다. B는 경제학 연구들이 대체로 새 경기장의 지역 경제 순효과가 작다고 본다는 점(지출이 다른 여가 소비에서 옮겨 올 뿐이라는 점)을 들어 핵심을 직접 다루며 사실관계도 맞다. 2) 오답: A의 자부심과 즐거움은 실재하지만 공공 자금을 써야 하는 이유로는 측정하기 어렵고 약하다. C의 건설 일자리는 공사 기간에만 있는 일시적 효과다. D는 일부 팬의 행동이라는 부차적 문제로, 경기장 재원 문제의 중심이 아니다. → 정답 B

items.stimulus: Tickets for the choir concert at the Merrowgate Harbour Festival cost $30 for an adult and $15 for a child under 16. Anyone buying 10 or more tickets in one purchase receives 20% off the total. Members of the festival choir may buy extra tickets for other people at 10% off. Discounts cannot be combined: when more than one discount applies to a purchase, only the larger one is given. No other discounts are available.
items.question: Place Yes if the conclusion follows. Place No if the conclusion does not follow.

statements.text: A group buying 10 adult tickets in one purchase pays $240 in total.
A choir member buying two adult tickets for friends pays $54 in total.
Two adults and two children who are not choir members, buying their four tickets together, pay $80 in total.
A choir member buying 10 adult tickets for friends in one purchase pays $270 in total.
A group buying 9 child tickets in one purchase pays $135 in total.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 1번: 10장이므로 20% 할인, 30 × 10 × 0.8 = 240달러로 맞다. 2번: 합창단원 할인 10%, 30 × 2 × 0.9 = 54달러로 맞다. 2) 3번: 4장이라 단체 할인이 없고 30 × 2 + 15 × 2 = 90달러이므로 80달러가 아니다. 3) 4번: 합창단원 할인(10%)과 단체 할인(20%)이 모두 해당하지만 중복되지 않고 큰 쪽만 적용되므로 300 × 0.8 = 240달러다. 270달러는 10% 할인을 적용한 값이라 틀렸다. 5번: 9장은 10장 미만이라 할인이 없고 15 × 9 = 135달러로 맞다. → 정답 1 Yes, 2 Yes, 3 No, 4 No, 5 Yes

items.stimulus: Six florists, Agathe, Bronwen, Cosimo, Delphine, Evander and Fiorella, each decorate one of the six carriages of a train on the Dunmore Heritage Railway. The carriages are numbered 1 to 6 from the front, and each florist decorates exactly one carriage. Cosimo's carriage number is higher than Bronwen's. Delphine's carriage number is exactly two more than Agathe's. Evander decorates either the first or the last carriage. Fiorella and Cosimo decorate neighbouring carriages, and so do Bronwen and Delphine. Agathe's carriage number is lower than Cosimo's.
items.question: Which of the following must be true?

options.text: Fiorella's carriage number is higher than Cosimo's.
Bronwen's carriage number is one more than Agathe's.

items.explanation_ko: 1) Delphine = Agathe + 2이고 Bronwen은 Delphine과 이웃이므로 Bronwen은 Agathe + 1 또는 Agathe + 3이다. Bronwen이 Agathe + 3이면 Cosimo는 그보다 뒤, Fiorella는 Cosimo 옆이어야 하고 Evander는 맨 앞이나 맨 끝이어야 해서 6칸에 다 들어가지 않는다. 2) 따라서 Agathe, Bronwen, Delphine이 연속하고 그 뒤에 Cosimo·Fiorella가 붙는다. Evander가 1번이면 A2 B3 D4이고 C·F가 5·6, Evander가 6번이면 A1 B2 D3이고 C·F가 4·5로, 모두 네 가지 배치가 가능하다. 3) 네 배치 모두에서 Bronwen은 Agathe 바로 다음 번호다. 오답: A, B, D는 각각 일부 배치에서만 참이다. → 정답 C

items.stimulus: While waiting at the Tarrow Ferry Terminal, 60 cyclists answered two questions. Their answers are shown as a two-circle Venn diagram. Circle P is 'rode more than 20 km today' and circle Q is 'carrying panniers'. The diagram shows 14 cyclists in P only, 11 in both P and Q, 18 in Q only and 17 outside both circles. In the statements, 'most' means more than half.
items.question: Place Yes if the conclusion follows. Place No if the conclusion does not follow.

statements.text: More than half of the 60 cyclists were carrying panniers.
Most of the cyclists who rode more than 20 km today were carrying panniers.
Fewer than a third of the 60 cyclists were outside both circles.
The number of cyclists in exactly one circle was more than three times the number in both circles.
Of the cyclists carrying panniers, fewer than 40% rode more than 20 km today.

items.explanation_ko: 1) Q(가방) 전체는 11 + 18 = 29명, P(20 km 초과) 전체는 14 + 11 = 25명이다. 2) 1번: 29명은 60명의 절반(30명)보다 적다. 2번: P 25명 중 가방을 든 사람은 11명으로 44%라 과반이 아니다. 3번: 바깥 17명은 60명의 3분의 1(20명)보다 적으므로 성립한다. 3) 4번: 한 원에만 있는 사람은 14 + 18 = 32명이고 둘 다는 11명이다. 11 × 3 = 33이므로 32는 세 배보다 많지 않다. 5번: 11 ÷ 29 = 약 37.9%로 40% 미만이다. → 정답 1 No, 2 No, 3 Yes, 4 No, 5 Yes

items.stimulus: Rules for the boating lake at the Quillon Botanic Garden: rowing boats may be hired between 9 am and 5 pm, and every boat must be back at the jetty by 5:30 pm. Each boat holds no more than three people. A child under 12 must be accompanied by an adult in the same boat. Everyone under 16 must wear a life jacket; people aged 16 or over may choose whether to wear one. The hire fee is $12 per boat for each hour or part of an hour.
items.question: Place Yes if the conclusion follows. Place No if the conclusion does not follow.

statements.text: A 14-year-old in a hired boat may choose not to wear a life jacket.
Two adults and two children may share one hired boat.
A group that keeps one boat for 90 minutes pays a hire fee of $18.
A 10-year-old may not row a hired boat alone.
Every adult in a hired boat must wear a life jacket.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 1번: 16세 미만은 반드시 구명조끼를 입어야 하므로 14세는 선택할 수 없다. 2번: 한 배에 최대 3명인데 4명이므로 안 된다. 2) 3번: 요금은 '1시간 또는 그 일부'마다 12달러라서 90분은 2시간분, 24달러다. 18달러는 시간 비례로 계산한 잘못된 값이다. 3) 4번: 12세 미만은 같은 배에 성인이 동승해야 하므로 10세 혼자 탈 수 없다는 결론이 따라 나온다. 5번: 16세 이상은 착용 여부를 선택할 수 있으므로 성인 모두가 입어야 한다는 결론은 틀렸다. → 정답 1 No, 2 No, 3 No, 4 Yes, 5 No

items.stimulus: Six tour guides from the Lowther Farmers' Cooperative, Hester, Ignatius, Juniper, Kasimir, Leocadia and Marguerite, sit around a circular table with six equally spaced seats. Juniper sits in the seat immediately clockwise from Hester. Ignatius sits directly opposite Hester. Marguerite sits next to Juniper. Leocadia does not sit next to Ignatius.
items.question: Who sits directly opposite Kasimir?
items.explanation_ko: 1) Hester 자리를 1번으로 두고 시계 방향으로 2~6번을 매긴다. Juniper는 Hester 바로 시계 방향인 2번, Ignatius는 Hester 맞은편인 4번이다. 2) Marguerite는 Juniper 옆인데 1번은 Hester이므로 3번이다. 남은 5·6번 중 Leocadia는 Ignatius(4번) 옆인 5번에 앉을 수 없으므로 6번, Kasimir는 5번이다. 3) 5번의 맞은편은 2번 Juniper다. 오답: Hester의 맞은편은 Ignatius, Marguerite(3번)의 맞은편은 Leocadia(6번)이므로 A, B, D는 Kasimir의 맞은편이 아니다. → 정답 C

items.stimulus: At the Saltmarsh Film Festival, a stallholder keeps raffle tickets in a box: 5 are red and 3 are blue. She draws two tickets at random, one after the other, without putting the first ticket back.
items.question: What is the probability that both tickets drawn are red?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 첫 장이 빨강일 확률은 5/8이다. 2) 첫 장을 되돌려 놓지 않으므로 남은 7장 중 빨강은 4장, 두 번째가 빨강일 확률은 4/7이다. 둘을 곱하면 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14이다. 3) 오답: B 25/64는 되돌려 놓는 경우(5/8 × 5/8)로 계산한 값, C 4/7은 두 번째 뽑기만 본 값, D 5/8은 첫 번째 뽑기만 본 값이다. → 정답 A

items.stimulus: On the Ashgrove Heritage Railway, no route pilot drives the steam locomotive. All drivers of the diesel shunter are route pilots. Every driver of the steam locomotive holds a boiler certificate. Some route pilots hold a boiler certificate.
items.question: Place Yes if the conclusion follows. Place No if the conclusion does not follow.

statements.text: Some drivers of the diesel shunter hold a boiler certificate.
No driver of the diesel shunter drives the steam locomotive.
Some people who hold a boiler certificate do not drive the steam locomotive.
Anyone who drives the steam locomotive is not a route pilot.
Every holder of a boiler certificate drives either the steam locomotive or the diesel shunter.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 디젤 운전자 ⊂ 루트 파일럿, 루트 파일럿과 증기 운전자는 겹치지 않음, 증기 운전자 ⊂ 보일러 자격자, 보일러 자격을 가진 루트 파일럿이 존재한다. 2) 1번: 보일러 자격을 가진 루트 파일럿이 디젤 운전자인지는 알 수 없어 따라 나오지 않는다. 2번: 디젤 운전자는 모두 루트 파일럿이고 루트 파일럿은 증기를 몰지 않으므로 성립한다. 3) 3번: 보일러 자격을 가진 루트 파일럿은 증기를 몰지 않으므로 성립한다. 4번: '어떤 루트 파일럿도 증기를 몰지 않는다'를 바꿔 말한 것이라 성립한다. 5번: 보일러 자격자가 두 기관차 중 하나를 꼭 운전한다는 정보는 없다. → 정답 1 No, 2 Yes, 3 Yes, 4 Yes, 5 No

items.stimulus: Fifty airline pilots on a layover visited the Corriemuir night market. A three-circle Venn diagram shows which of three foods each pilot bought: dumplings, satay and noodles. The diagram shows: dumplings only 8; satay only 6; noodles only 7; dumplings and satay only 4; dumplings and noodles only 3; satay and noodles only 5; all three 2; none of the three 15.
items.question: How many pilots bought exactly two of the three foods?
items.explanation_ko: 1) '정확히 두 가지'는 두 원만 겹치는 세 영역(셋째 원은 제외)이다. 2) 4 + 3 + 5 = 12명이다. 3) 오답: A 21은 한 가지만 산 사람(8 + 6 + 7), B 14는 세 가지 모두 산 2명을 '두 가지 이상'으로 함께 센 값, C 2는 세 가지를 모두 산 사람 수다. → 정답 D

items.stimulus: Five volunteers, Quillan, Rosalind, Sebastiano, Tamsin and Ulrike, each help at the Fairhaven River Regatta on a different weekday from Monday to Friday. Tamsin helps on Wednesday. Rosalind helps on the day after Quillan. Ulrike helps earlier in the week than Quillan. Sebastiano does not help on Monday.
items.question: Who helps on Friday?
items.explanation_ko: 1) 수요일은 Tamsin이다. Quillan과 Rosalind는 연속한 이틀이므로 (월, 화) 또는 (목, 금)이다. 2) Ulrike가 Quillan보다 먼저여야 하므로 Quillan은 월요일일 수 없다. 따라서 Quillan 목요일, Rosalind 금요일이다. 3) 남은 월·화 중 Sebastiano는 월요일이 아니므로 화요일, Ulrike는 월요일이다. 오답: Quillan은 목요일, Sebastiano는 화요일, Ulrike는 월요일이다. → 정답 D

items.stimulus: Three guests at the Coralline Island resort each try, independently, to row a small boat around the lagoon marker before lunch. The probabilities that they succeed are 0.5, 0.4 and 0.3.
items.question: What is the probability that at least one of the three guests succeeds?
items.explanation_ko: 1) '적어도 한 명 성공'은 '세 명 모두 실패'의 여사건이다. 2) 실패 확률은 각각 0.5, 0.6, 0.7이고 독립이므로 모두 실패할 확률은 0.5 × 0.6 × 0.7 = 0.21이다. 따라서 1 - 0.21 = 0.79이다. 3) 오답: A 0.06은 세 명 모두 성공할 확률(0.5 × 0.4 × 0.3), B 0.21은 모두 실패할 확률 자체, D 0.94는 1에서 '모두 성공'을 뺀 값으로 '적어도 한 명 실패'의 확률이다. → 정답 C

items.stimulus: Should smartphones carry health warnings about screen time?
items.question: Select the strongest argument from the statements below.

options.text: Yes, because health authorities in several countries advise limiting young children's screen time, and a warning would bring that advice to parents.
No, because there is no evidence at all that the amount of time people spend looking at screens has any effect on their health.
Yes, because smartphones are clearly the main cause of the rise in poor mental health among teenagers in many wealthy countries over the last fifteen years.
No, because people already ignore many of the warnings printed on everyday products, such as the labels on food packaging.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 쟁점은 경고 문구가 사용자에게 유용한 건강 정보를 전달하는가이다. A는 여러 나라의 보건 당국(health authorities in several countries)이 이미 어린 아이의 화면 시간을 제한하라고 권고하고 있다는 사실을 근거로, 경고가 그 권고를 부모에게 전달한다는 실제적 이익을 과장 없이 제시한다. 2) 오답: B는 '증거가 전혀 없다'는 과장으로 사실과 다르다. C는 스마트폰이 청소년 정신 건강 악화의 '명백한 주원인'이라고 단정하는데 이는 연구자들 사이에서도 논쟁 중인 주장이다. D는 일부 경고가 무시된다는 일반론일 뿐 경고가 아무 효과가 없다는 근거가 되지 못한다. → 정답 A

items.stimulus: At the Penhallow Ferry Terminal one morning: all of the chess players waiting there held tickets for the morning ferry. Some holders of morning-ferry tickets were tourists. None of the chess players was a tourist.
items.question: Which of the following diagrams best represents these statements?

options.text: The Chess circle lies inside the Morning circle, and the Tourist circle overlaps both the Chess and Morning circles.
The Chess and Morning circles partly overlap, and the Tourist circle overlaps the Morning circle only.
The Chess circle lies inside the Morning circle, and the Tourist circle lies completely outside the Morning circle.
The Chess circle lies inside the Morning circle, and the Tourist circle overlaps the Morning circle but not the Chess circle.

items.question: Henrike runs a fixed route at a steady pace of 5 minutes 0 seconds per kilometre. Tobiah starts from the same point 3 minutes after her and runs the same route at a steady 4 minutes 30 seconds per kilometre. How far from the start does Tobiah catch up with Henrike?
